claim: Dysfunction of the striatum is frequently associated with sleep disturbances.
source: Dysfunction of the striatum is frequently associated with sleep disturbances.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract without specific data or citations provided in this sentence.

claim: The striatum densely expresses adenosine A2A receptors (A2ARs).
source: the striatum densely expresses adenosine A2A receptors (A2ARs)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the striatum.

claim: A2ARs are essential for adenosine-induced sleep.
source: adenosine A2A receptors (A2ARs), which are essential for adenosine-induced sleep
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, though citations are provided elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of A2AR neurons in specific subregions of the striatum induced a remarkable increase in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep.
source: chemogenetic activation of A2AR neurons in specific subregions of the striatum induced a remarkable increase in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Striatal A2AR neurons innervated the external globus pallidus (GPe) in a topographically organized manner.
source: Anatomical mapping and immunoelectron microscopy revealed that striatal A2AR neurons innervated the external globus pallidus (GPe) in a topographically organized manner
evidence: This is supported by anatomical mapping data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Striatal A2AR neurons preferentially formed inhibitory synapses with GPe parvalbumin (PV) neurons.
source: striatal A2AR neurons innervated the external globus pallidus (GPe) in a topographically organized manner and preferentially formed inhibitory synapses with GPe parvalbumin (PV) neurons
evidence: This is supported by immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Lesions of GPe PV neurons abolished the sleep-promoting effect of striatal A2AR neurons.
source: lesions of GPe PV neurons abolished the sleep-promoting effect of striatal A2AR neurons
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of striatal A2AR neurons led to a significant decrease of NREM sleep at active period, but not inactive period of mice.
source: chemogenetic inhibition of striatal A2AR neurons led to a significant decrease of NREM sleep at active period, but not inactive period of mice
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The striatum serves as the primary input nucleus of the basal ganglia.
source: the striatum (caudate putamen), which resides in the forebrain and serves as the primary input nucleus of the basal ganglia
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The striatum is involved in motor control, habit formation, and goal-directed behaviors.
source: the striatum (caudate putamen), which resides in the forebrain and serves as the primary input nucleus of the basal ganglia, is involved in an array of physiological processes including motor control, habit formation, and goal-directed behaviors (Durieux et al., 2011; Graybiel, 2008; Li et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Up to 90% of patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) exhibit severe sleep disturbances.
source: Up to 90% of patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) exhibit severe sleep disturbances, which is one of the most frequent non-motor symptoms (Arnulf et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc) projects primarily to the striatum.
source: the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), which projects primarily to the striatum
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The SNc is the major area of degeneration in PD.
source: the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), which projects primarily to the striatum, is the major area of degeneration in PD
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Parkinson's disease pathology.

claim: Dysfunction of the striatum may contribute to sleep disturbances in PD patients.
source: dysfunction of the striatum may contribute to sleep disturbances in PD patients
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the connection between SNc degeneration and striatal function.

claim: Few studies have examined the role of the striatum in sleep-wake regulation.
source: to date, few studies have examined the role of the striatum in sleep-wake regulation
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: Surgical removal of the striatum in cats decreases time spent in sleep.
source: surgical removal of the striatum in cats (Villablanca, 1972) and striatal excitotoxic lesions in rats (Mena-Segovia et al., 2002) decrease time spent in sleep
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Striatal excitotoxic lesions in rats decrease time spent in sleep.
source: surgical removal of the striatum in cats (Villablanca, 1972) and striatal excitotoxic lesions in rats (Mena-Segovia et al., 2002) decrease time spent in sleep
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Electrical lesion of the rat striatum selectively increases rapid eye movement (REM) sleep.
source: electrical lesion of the rat striatum selectively increases rapid eye movement (REM) sleep (Corsi-Cabrera et al., 1975)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Lesion of the striatum by ibotenic acid induces an increase in NREM sleep and a decrease in REM sleep.
source: lesion by ibotenic acid induces an increase in the non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and a decrease in the REM sleep (Qiu et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cerebral blood flow in caudate nucleus increases during REM sleep.
source: a H215O PET study shows that cerebral blood flow (represents activity of the brain) in caudate nucleus, which is equivalent to the rostral striatum of rodents (Kreitzer, 2009), increases during REM sleep and decreases during slow-wave sleep (Braun et al., 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cerebral blood flow in caudate nucleus decreases during slow-wave sleep.
source: a H215O PET study shows that cerebral blood flow (represents activity of the brain) in caudate nucleus, which is equivalent to the rostral striatum of rodents (Kreitzer, 2009), increases during REM sleep and decreases during slow-wave sleep (Braun et al., 1997)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The caudate nucleus is equivalent to the rostral striatum of rodents.
source: caudate nucleus, which is equivalent to the rostral striatum of rodents (Kreitzer, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The striatum contains GABAergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs, 95%) and interneurons (5%).
source: The striatum contains GABAergic medium spiny neurons (MSNs, 95%) and interneurons (5%) (Kreitzer, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: MSNs are divided into two projection neuron classes.
source: MSNs are divided into two projection neuron classes
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about striatal anatomy.

claim: Striatopallidal neurons express adenosine A2A receptors (A2ARs) and dopamine D2 receptors (D2Rs).
source: One class consists of striatopallidal neurons that express the adenosine A2A receptors (A2ARs) and dopamine D2 receptors (D2Rs), and project to the external globus pallidus (GPe)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about striatal neuron types.

claim: Striatopallidal neurons project to the external globus pallidus (GPe).
source: One class consists of striatopallidal neurons that express the adenosine A2A receptors (A2ARs) and dopamine D2 receptors (D2Rs), and project to the external globus pallidus (GPe)
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about striatal projections.

claim: Striatonigral neurons express adenosine A1 receptors (A1Rs) and dopamine D1 receptors (D1Rs).
source: The other class consists of striatonigral neurons that express adenosine A1 receptors (A1Rs) and dopamine D1 receptors (D1Rs), and project primarily to the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) and the internal globus pallidus (GPi) (Kreitzer, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Striatonigral neurons project primarily to the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) and the internal globus pallidus (GPi).
source: The other class consists of striatonigral neurons that express adenosine A1 receptors (A1Rs) and dopamine D1 receptors (D1Rs), and project primarily to the substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) and the internal globus pallidus (GPi) (Kreitzer, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Both A1Rs and A2ARs have been reported to regulate sleep.
source: Both A1Rs and A2ARs have been reported to regulate sleep (Basheer et al., 2004; Thakkar et al., 2003; Urade et al., 2003)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A1Rs contribute to sleep induction in a region-dependent manner.
source: A1Rs contribute to sleep induction in a region-dependent manner, whereas A2ARs play a predominant role in sleep induction (Huang et al., 2005; Lazarus et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A2ARs play a predominant role in sleep induction.
source: A1Rs contribute to sleep induction in a region-dependent manner, whereas A2ARs play a predominant role in sleep induction (Huang et al., 2005; Lazarus et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The expression level of A2ARs is altered in the striatum of PD patients.
source: it has been reported that the expression level of A2ARs is altered in the striatum of PD patients (Mishina et al., 2011; Ramlackhansingh et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Altered A2AR expression may change the activity of striatal A2AR neurons.
source: the expression level of A2ARs is altered in the striatum of PD patients (Mishina et al., 2011; Ramlackhansingh et al., 2011), which may change the activity of striatal A2AR neurons (Gerfen et al., 1990; Mitchell et al., 1989)
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Altered striatal A2AR neuron activity may contribute to sleep disturbances in PD patients.
source: the expression level of A2ARs is altered in the striatum of PD patients (Mishina et al., 2011; Ramlackhansingh et al., 2011), which may change the activity of striatal A2AR neurons (Gerfen et al., 1990; Mitchell et al., 1989), thus contributing to sleep disturbances in PD patients
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on previous findings.

claim: CNO injection caused robust c-fos expression in hM3Dq-expressing A2AR neurons.
source: intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of the specific hM3Dq ligand, clozapine-N-oxide (CNO, 1 mg/kg), but not vehicle, dramatically drove c-fos expression in hM3Dq-expressing A2AR neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: CNO perfusion induced depolarization and firing of hM3Dq-expressing A2AR neurons in the striatum.
source: whole-cell current-clamp recordings showed that a brief CNO (5 μM) perfusion induced depolarization and firing of hM3Dq-expressing A2AR neurons in the striatum and the effect was reversible following CNO washout (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CNO application had no effect on membrane potential and firing of non-hM3Dq-expressing neurons in the striatum in vitro.
source: CNO application had no effect on membrane potential and firing of non-hM3Dq-expressing neurons in the striatum in vitro (data not shown)
evidence: This is stated as an experimental result, though data are not shown.

claim: CNO had no effect on sleep-wake profiles of non-hM3Dq-expressing mice in vivo.
source: CNO application had no effect on membrane potential and firing of non-hM3Dq-expressing neurons in the striatum in vitro (data not shown) and sleep-wake profiles of non-hM3Dq-expressing mice in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: CNO injection increased NREM sleep by 2.2-fold in mice expressing hM3Dq receptors in the rostral striatum.
source: The amount of CNO-induced NREM sleep was significantly increased by 2.2-fold during the 3 hr post-injection period as compared with vehicle (Figure 1I)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: CNO injection decreased wakefulness by 32% in mice expressing hM3Dq receptors in the rostral striatum.
source: the amount of wakefulness was significantly decreased by 32% following administration of CNO (Figure 1B, C and J)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1B, C and J.

claim: CNO injection did not significantly change REM sleep in mice expressing hM3Dq receptors in the rostral striatum.
source: REM sleep was not significantly changed (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and E)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and E.

claim: CNO injection increased the mean duration of NREM sleep in mice expressing hM3Dq receptors in the rostral striatum.
source: CNO injection induced an increase in the mean duration of NREM sleep with a decrease in wakefulness, and had no effect on the episode numbers of 3 vigilance stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: CNO injection decreased the mean duration of wakefulness in mice expressing hM3Dq receptors in the rostral striatum.
source: CNO injection induced an increase in the mean duration of NREM sleep with a decrease in wakefulness, and had no effect on the episode numbers of 3 vigilance stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: CNO injection had no effect on the episode numbers of 3 vigilance stages in mice expressing hM3Dq receptors in the rostral striatum.
source: CNO injection induced an increase in the mean duration of NREM sleep with a decrease in wakefulness, and had no effect on the episode numbers of 3 vigilance stages (Figure 1—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of A2AR neurons in the rostral striatum did not change EEG power density of NREM sleep.
source: no change was detected in EEG power density of NREM sleep during the 3 hr post-CNO injection as compared with vehicle (Figure 1D)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The increased sleep induced by activation of A2AR neurons in the rostral striatum was similar to a physiological sleep pattern.
source: no change was detected in EEG power density of NREM sleep during the 3 hr post-CNO injection as compared with vehicle (Figure 1D), which suggests that the increased sleep was similar to a physiological sleep pattern
evidence: This is an inference based on the EEG power density data.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of A2AR neurons in the centromedial striatum increased NREM sleep by 2.2-fold.
source: chemogenetic activation of A2AR neurons in the centromedial or centrolateral striatum increased NREM sleep by 2.2-fold and 1.8-fold, respectively (Figure 1I and J and Figure 1—figure supplements 3B, C, F, G, 4 and 5)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1I and J and supplementary figures.

claim: Chemogenetic activation of A2AR neurons in the centrolateral striatum increased NREM sleep by 1.8-fold.
source: chemogenetic activation of A2AR neurons in the centromedial or centrolateral striatum increased NREM sleep by 2.2-fold and 1.8-fold, respectively (Figure 1I and J and Figure 1—figure supplements 3B, C, F, G, 4 and 5)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1I and J and supplementary figures.

claim: A2AR neurons in the rostral, centromedial, and centrolateral but not caudal striatum are involved in sleep-wake regulation.
source: These results indicate that A2AR neurons in the rostral, centromedial, and centrolateral but not caudal striatum are involved in sleep-wake regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from Figure 1.

claim: hrGFP-expressing neurons displayed typical morphology of MSNs in the striatum.
source: we found that hrGFP-expressing neurons displayed typical morphology of MSNs (Figure 2B) in the striatum
evidence: This is supported by morphological data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: hrGFP-expressing neurons showed positive signals for A2AR immunoreactivity.
source: hrGFP-expressing neurons displayed typical morphology of MSNs (Figure 2B) in the striatum, and positive signals for A2AR immunoreactivity (Figure 2C–F)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C–F.

claim: Axons of A2AR neurons in the rostral striatum were found in the rostral GPe with a discoidal field paralleling the strio-pallidal border.
source: axons of A2AR neurons in the rostral striatum were found in the rostral GPe with a discoidal field paralleling the strio-pallidal border (Figure 2G)
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Axons from the central striatum were distributed in both the rostral and caudal GPe.
source: Axons from the central striatum were distributed not only in the rostral but also the caudal GPe, forming similar discoidal areas paralleling the strio-pallidal border (Figure 2G)
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Axons from the caudal striatum were distributed only in the caudal GPe.
source: axons from the caudal striatum were distributed only in the caudal GPe (Figure 2G)
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Axons of the lateral striatum projected preferentially to the lateral GPe.
source: it is notable that axons of the lateral striatum projected preferentially to the lateral GPe
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the anatomical mapping.

claim: The projections of A2AR neurons in different subregions of the striatum are organized topographically in the GPe.
source: These findings indicate that the projections of A2AR neurons in different subregions of the striatum are organized topographically in the GPe
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the anatomical mapping data.

claim: The topographical projections of A2AR neurons may contribute to the discrepancies in A2AR neuron-mediated sleep.
source: the projections of A2AR neurons in different subregions of the striatum are organized topographically in the GPe and suggest that the topographical projections of A2AR neurons may contribute to the discrepancies in A2AR neuron-mediated sleep
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the anatomical findings.

claim: hrGFP-IR terminals established symmetric synapses with dendrites labeled for PV.
source: We observed that hrGFP-IR terminals established symmetric synapses with dendrites that were labeled or unlabeled for PV (Figure 2H and J)
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2H and J.

claim: hrGFP-IR terminals established symmetric synapses with dendrites unlabeled for PV.
source: We observed that hrGFP-IR terminals established symmetric synapses with dendrites that were labeled or unlabeled for PV (Figure 2H and J)
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2H and J.

claim: A small number of perikarya labeled for PV received symmetric synapses from hrGFP-IR terminals.
source: a small number of perikarya, which were labeled or unlabeled for PV, received symmetric synapses from hrGFP-IR terminals (Figure 2I and K)
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2I and K.

claim: A small number of perikarya unlabeled for PV received symmetric synapses from hrGFP-IR terminals.
source: a small number of perikarya, which were labeled or unlabeled for PV, received symmetric synapses from hrGFP-IR terminals (Figure 2I and K)
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2I and K.

claim: hrGFP-labeled terminals formed significantly more synapses with PV-IR profiles than PV-unlabeled profiles (81.2% vs. 18.8%) in the rostral GPe.
source: hrGFP-labeled terminals formed significantly more synapses with PV-IR profiles than PV-unlabeled profiles (81.2% vs. 18.8%, n = 377 synapses from five mice; Figure 2L) in the rostral GPe
evidence: This is supported by quantitative electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: In the caudal GPe, hrGFP-IR terminals preferentially formed synapses with PV-unlabeled profiles than PV-labeled profiles (61.3% vs. 38.7%).
source: In contrast, in the caudal GPe, hrGFP-IR terminals preferentially formed synapses with PV-unlabeled profiles than PV-labeled profiles (61.3% vs. 38.7%, n = 275 synapses from five mice; Figure 2L)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: A2AR neurons in the rostral striatum preferentially form symmetric synapses with PV-positive neurons in the rostral GPe.
source: These anatomical findings indicate that A2AR neurons in the rostral striatum preferentially form symmetric synapses with PV-positive neurons in the rostral GPe
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electron microscopy data.

claim: A2AR neurons in the caudal striatum preferentially form synapses with PV-negative neurons in the caudal GPe.
source: A2AR neurons in the caudal striatum preferentially form synapses with PV-negative neurons in the caudal GPe
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electron microscopy data.

claim: There is a rostral-caudal variation in striatopallidal connections.
source: These anatomical findings indicate that A2AR neurons in the rostral striatum preferentially form symmetric synapses with PV-positive neurons in the rostral GPe, while A2AR neurons in the caudal striatum preferentially form synapses with PV-negative neurons in the caudal GPe, indicating a rostral-caudal variation in striatopallidal connections
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electron microscopy data.

claim: Photostimulation of cell bodies of A2AR neurons elicited robust photocurrents.
source: Photostimulation of cell bodies of A2AR neurons elicited robust photocurrents (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Trains of brief blue light flashes evoked single action potentials at frequencies of 5–30 Hz with high fidelity in A2AR neurons.
source: trains of brief blue light flashes (1–3 ms) evoked single action potentials at frequencies of 5–30 Hz with high fidelity (Figure 3—figure supplement 1J–M)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1J–M.

claim: Photostimulation decreased the firing rate of most PV-positive neurons to 58% of the spontaneous firing rate.
source: photostimulation decreased the firing rate of most PV-positive neurons, which showed immunoreactive signals for PV but not FoxP2 (Figure 3B and C), to 58% of the spontaneous firing rate (from 30.3 ± 2.9 to 17.6 ± 2.6 Hz, n = 19 from 10 mice; Figure 3D–F)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: The firing rate of PV-positive neurons recovered immediately when photostimulation was terminated.
source: photostimulation decreased the firing rate of most PV-positive neurons, which showed immunoreactive signals for PV but not FoxP2 (Figure 3B and C), to 58% of the spontaneous firing rate (from 30.3 ± 2.9 to 17.6 ± 2.6 Hz, n = 19 from 10 mice; Figure 3D–F), and the firing rate recovered immediately when photostimulation was terminated
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3D–F.

claim: Photostimulation decreased the firing rate of PV-negative neurons to 25% of the spontaneous firing rate.
source: In PV-negative neurons which were FoxP2-IR (Figure 3G and H), photostimulation decreased the firing rate to 25% of the spontaneous firing rate (from 9.2 ± 0.9 to 2.3 ± 0.8 Hz, n = 12 from 10 mice; Figure 3I–K)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3I–K.

claim: A rebound in the firing rate after photostimulation was observed in 6 of 12 PV-negative neurons.
source: Notably, a rebound in the firing rate after photostimulation was observed in 6 of 12 PV-negative neurons (10 mice)
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Flashes of blue light evoked fast inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) in both PV-positive and PV-negative neurons.
source: flashes of blue light evoked fast inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) in both PV-positive and PV-negative neurons (Figure 3F and K) with a latency of less than 5 ms (Figure 3N)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3F, K, and N.

claim: Light-evoked IPSCs had a latency of less than 5 ms, indicating a direct connection between terminals of A2AR neurons and PV-positive or PV-negative neurons.
source: flashes of blue light evoked fast inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) in both PV-positive and PV-negative neurons (Figure 3F and K) with a latency of less than 5 ms (Figure 3N), indicating a direct connection between terminals of A2AR neurons and PV-positive or PV-negative neurons
evidence: This is an inference based on the short latency of the IPSCs.

claim: Light-evoked IPSCs were completely abolished by picrotoxin (PTX, 100 μM).
source: the light-evoked IPSCs were completely abolished by picrotoxin (PTX, 100 μM; Figure 3F and K)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3F and K.

claim: Light-evoked IPSCs were mediated by GABA released from axon terminals of A2AR neurons and postsynaptic GABAA receptors on GPe neurons.
source: the light-evoked IPSCs were completely abolished by picrotoxin (PTX, 100 μM; Figure 3F and K), indicating that these responses were mediated by GABA released from axon terminals of A2AR neurons and postsynaptic GABAA receptors on GPe neurons
evidence: This is an inference based on the effect of PTX, a GABAA receptor antagonist.

claim: Light-evoked IPSCs were recorded in 76% of neurons (45 of 59 neurons from 10 mice) in the rostral GPe.
source: light-evoked IPSCs were recorded in 76% of neurons (45 of 59 neurons from 10 mice) in the rostral GPe, and 53% of neurons (10 of 19 neurons from 5 mice) in the caudal GPe (Figure 3L)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Light-evoked IPSCs were recorded in 53% of neurons (10 of 19 neurons from 5 mice) in the caudal GPe.
source: light-evoked IPSCs were recorded in 76% of neurons (45 of 59 neurons from 10 mice) in the rostral GPe, and 53% of neurons (10 of 19 neurons from 5 mice) in the caudal GPe (Figure 3L)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: The amplitude of the first IPSC evoked by blue light flashes at 10 Hz was significantly larger in PV-positive neurons than in PV-negative neurons in the rostral GPe.
source: the amplitude of the first IPSC evoked by blue light flashes at 10 Hz was significantly larger in PV-positive neurons than in PV-negative neurons (860.4 ± 157.3 pA, n = 23 vs. 234.3 ± 69.7 pA, n = 18, from 10 mice) in the rostral GPe (Figure 3M)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Connections between terminals of A2AR neurons and PV-positive neurons were not detected in the caudal GPe, possibly due to their low numbers in this region.
source: we did not detect connections between terminals of A2AR neurons and PV-positive neuron in the caudal GPe, possibly due to their low numbers in this region
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a speculative explanation.

claim: Striatal A2AR neurons preferentially innervate and inhibit PV neurons in the rostral GPe.
source: these data support anatomical studies indicating that striatal A2AR neurons preferentially innervate and inhibit PV neurons in the rostral GPe
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electrophysiological and anatomical data.

claim: Light stimulation of ChR2-expressing A2AR neuron terminals in the GPe remarkably increased NREM sleep by 1.8-fold.
source: Light stimulation for 1 hr with optical fiber implanted into the GPe, containing ChR2-expressing A2AR neuron terminals, remarkably increased NREM sleep by 1.8-fold (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Striatal A2AR neurons promoted sleep by inhibiting neurons, more likely PV neurons, in the GPe.
source: Light stimulation for 1 hr with optical fiber implanted into the GPe, containing ChR2-expressing A2AR neuron terminals, remarkably increased NREM sleep by 1.8-fold (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), strongly suggesting that striatal A2AR neurons promoted sleep by inhibiting neurons, more likely PV neurons, in the GPe
evidence: This is an inference based on the optogenetic stimulation data.

claim: Bath application of CNO (5 μM) reduced the spontaneous firing rate of PV neurons expressing hM4Di receptors in the GPe.
source: Bath application of CNO (5 μM) reduced the spontaneous firing rate of PV neurons expressing hM4Di receptors in the GPe (Figure 4D)
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CNO (1 mg/kg, i.p.) injections caused mice to fall asleep with an increased NREM sleep and decreased wakefulness, and this effect was sustained for 3 hr.
source: Systemically, CNO (1 mg/kg, i.p.) injections caused mice to fall asleep with an increased NREM sleep and decreased wakefulness, and this effect was sustained for 3 hr (Figure 4E–G)
evidence: This is supported by sleep-wake monitoring data shown in Figure 4E–G.

claim: The amount of CNO-induced NREM sleep was significantly increased by 1.6-fold with a decrease in wake by 26% during the 3 hr post-injection period in mice expressing hM4Di in GPe PV neurons.
source: The amount of CNO-induced NREM sleep was significantly increased by 1.6-fold with a decrease in wake by 26% during the 3 hr post-injection period as compared with vehicle (Figure 4F and G)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: CNO injection did not alter REM sleep in mice expressing hM4Di in GPe PV neurons.
source: However, REM sleep (Figure 4F and G), the latency to the first NREM sleep and EEG power density of NREM sleep (Figure 4H) during the 3 hr post-CNO injection was not altered
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F, G, and H.

claim: CNO injection did not alter the latency to the first NREM sleep in mice expressing hM4Di in GPe PV neurons.
source: However, REM sleep (Figure 4F and G), the latency to the first NREM sleep and EEG power density of NREM sleep (Figure 4H) during the 3 hr post-CNO injection was not altered
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F, G, and H.

claim: CNO injection did not alter EEG power density of NREM sleep in mice expressing hM4Di in GPe PV neurons.
source: However, REM sleep (Figure 4F and G), the latency to the first NREM sleep and EEG power density of NREM sleep (Figure 4H) during the 3 hr post-CNO injection was not altered
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F, G, and H.

claim: Inhibition of PV neurons in the GPe mimics the effect of activation of striatal A2AR neurons.
source: These findings demonstrate that inhibition of PV neurons in the GPe mimics the effect of activation of striatal A2AR neurons
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of experimental results.

claim: PV neurons of the GPe are a critical downstream target for striatal A2AR neuron-mediated sleep.
source: These findings demonstrate that inhibition of PV neurons in the GPe mimics the effect of activation of striatal A2AR neurons and confirm PV neurons of the GPe as a critical downstream target for striatal A2AR neuron-mediated sleep
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: Microinjection of taCasp3 vector significantly decreased the number of PV-IR neurons in the GPe compared with the control group.
source: We found that microinjection of taCasp3 vector significantly decreased the number of PV-IR and HuCD-IR neurons compared with the control group (p<0.001; Figure 5E–G)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5E–G.
